## Scope

This review sets out to survey the field of membrane separations for solvent recovery, drawing together a body of literature that has grown considerably in recent years. In total, the review covers 140 papers from the last 11 years, encompassing laboratory studies, pilot demonstrations and a smaller number of reports from industrial practice. The scope is deliberately restricted to membranes used for the recovery of organic solvents from process streams, and it includes both polymeric and ceramic membranes, as well as the hybrid configurations that have begun to appear in the literature. Studies concerned purely with aqueous separations fall outside the scope, as do patents and manufacturers' literature, which are not subject to the same scrutiny as the peer-reviewed work on which this review is based.

## Established results

There are several findings on which the literature is now in broad agreement, and these can be regarded as established. It is well established, firstly, that solvent-resistant membranes can maintain useful selectivity over extended periods in a number of the milder solvent environments, and that the catastrophic loss of performance that was once feared in organic media is not the general rule. Secondly, there is a consensus that the swelling of the membrane material by the solvent is the central phenomenon governing performance, since swelling alters both the transport of the solvent itself and the rejection of dissolved species, and it is now widely accepted that membrane screening carried out in one solvent cannot simply be read across to another. Thirdly, it has become clear that the economics of membrane solvent recovery are most favourable where the membrane unit displaces a thermal separation duty rather than competing with one that is already efficient, and that the strongest cases are those in which the recovered solvent has a high value or the stream would otherwise incur a disposal cost.

In addition to these general findings, the literature provides a reasonably consistent picture of the way in which performance responds to operating conditions. Increases in pressure are reported to raise solvent flux, although the benefit is frequently offset by compaction of the membrane structure, and increases in temperature are reported to reduce rejection in many polymeric systems as the material swells and the transport of solutes becomes easier. Cross-flow operation is consistently reported to mitigate the accumulation of rejected material at the membrane surface, and the practice of staging membrane units so that the retentate passes through successive units is well documented in the larger studies. On these points, at least, the reader can proceed with some confidence.

## Disagreements

Against this background, however, there remains one important quantity on which the published reports come into direct conflict with one another, and that quantity is the decline in solvent flux during extended operation. A substantial group of studies reports that flux settles, after an initial settling-in period, to a value that is then maintained more or less indefinitely, and these studies present the membrane as being essentially stable in service. Another substantial group, working with what appear to be comparable membranes and comparable solvents, reports a continuing and progressive decline in flux that shows no sign of levelling off within the duration of the experiments described. Both positions cannot be correct as general statements about the same class of materials, and yet each is supported by a body of careful work.

A variety of explanations have been put forward for this discrepancy. It has been suggested that the difference lies in the pretreatment of the feed, in the presence or absence of trace contaminants that adsorb on the membrane, in the cleaning regimes applied between runs, and in the simple matter of how long the experiments were allowed to run. Studies reporting stability have tended to be shorter than studies reporting decline, which raises the uncomfortable possibility that the stable picture is an artefact of duration. Equally, it has been argued that the declining picture reflects contaminants present in real process streams that are absent from the cleaner model mixtures used elsewhere, so that the disagreement may not be about the membrane at all, but rather about the stream to which it was exposed. At the present time, the literature does not contain the controlled, side-by-side comparison that would be needed in order to resolve the matter, and the reader is left to weigh the two bodies of evidence against each other.

## Gaps

Finally, there are significant gaps in the literature that deserve to be highlighted. The most striking of these concerns a measurement that, remarkably, nobody appears to report: the solvent flux of a membrane measured after repeated cleaning cycles at module scale. Individual studies report flux before and after a single cleaning, and a great many studies report flux on small membrane coupons that have never been cleaned at all, but the cumulative effect of cleaning on the performance of a full module, which is the form in which the technology would actually be deployed, is essentially absent from the record. This is a serious omission, because cleaning is one of the principal operating costs of a membrane plant, and a membrane that recovers its flux fully after each of many cleanings is a very different proposition from one that loses a little performance with every cycle.

Related gaps appear elsewhere in the record. Long-duration studies remain rare relative to the number of short screening studies, and reports of performance on genuine process streams, as opposed to synthetic mixtures prepared for the laboratory, are rarer still. Information about the condition of membranes after service, and about the mechanisms by which they eventually fail, is seldom provided. Until these gaps are filled, assessments of the technology for solvent recovery will continue to rest on a foundation that is narrower than the confidence of much of the writing in the field would suggest.

It is also worth noting, by way of context, that the literature surveyed here reflects what researchers have chosen to investigate and to publish, which is not necessarily the same thing as what industry has chosen to install. Duties that were taken into operation without any accompanying publication do not appear in the record, and neither do duties that were abandoned at an early stage, so that the picture presented by the literature may be systematically more favourable than the picture that would be given by a survey of operating plants, if such a survey could somehow be carried out.

None of this should be taken to diminish the value of the work that has been done. The field has established a great deal in a comparatively short period, and the techniques involved are now understood far better than they were. Nevertheless, the combination of a live disagreement about long-term behaviour and a set of gaps concentrated in exactly the areas that matter most for industrial deployment means that considerable caution is still called for, and it is hoped that this review will assist readers in directing that caution to the places where it is most needed.

## Scope

The review covers 140 papers from the last 11 years on membrane separations for solvent recovery. The scope is membranes used to recover organic solvents from process streams: polymeric membranes, ceramic membranes, and the hybrid configurations that combine them. Work on aqueous separations stands outside the scope, as do patents and manufacturers' literature, which are not examined by the review process applied to the journal papers. Reports are laboratory studies in the main, with pilot demonstrations a minority and reports from industrial practice a small minority.

## Established results

Three results are established across the literature. Solvent-resistant membranes maintain useful selectivity over extended periods in the milder solvent environments, and the rapid destruction of performance in organic media that early work led readers to expect is not the general rule. Swelling of the membrane material by the solvent governs performance: swelling changes the transport of the solvent and the rejection of dissolved species together, and screening results obtained in one solvent do not transfer to another. The economics are strongest where the membrane unit displaces a thermal separation duty, and strongest of all where the recovered solvent has a high value or the stream would otherwise carry a disposal cost.

The response of performance to operating conditions is also consistent across reports. Raising the pressure raises solvent flux, with part of the gain lost to compaction of the membrane structure. Raising the temperature lowers rejection in many polymeric systems, as the material swells and solute transport becomes easier. Cross-flow operation reduces the accumulation of rejected material at the membrane surface, and staging units so that the retentate passes through successive units is documented in the larger studies. On these points the reports agree in direction, and differ mainly in magnitude.

## Disagreements

Reports conflict on one quantity: the decline in solvent flux during extended operation. One body of studies reports that flux falls during an initial period and then holds at a level value for the remaining duration of the work. Another body, on membranes and solvents that appear comparable, reports a flux that continues to decline throughout the run and shows no approach to a level value. The two accounts cannot both hold as general descriptions of the same materials in the same duty.

The candidate explanations are visible in the reports themselves. The studies differ in feed pretreatment, in the trace contaminants available to adsorb on the membrane, in the cleaning applied between runs, and in duration. The studies reporting stable flux are in general shorter than the studies reporting decline, which leaves open the possibility that the stable account is an artefact of duration: a run that ends during the level period of a slow decline reports stability. The studies reporting decline more often used real process streams, which leaves open the opposite possibility, that the decline belongs to the contaminants of a real stream and not to the membrane. No study in the set runs the same membrane on the same stream under both cleaning regimes for long enough to separate these explanations, and the disagreement is therefore a disagreement about confounded variables, stated in the literature as a disagreement about membranes. The limited preference the evidence supports is conditional: on clean, prepared feeds, flux after the initial period is stable in most reports; on unprepared process streams, a continuing decline is the safer planning assumption.

## Gaps

One measurement is absent from the whole set: the solvent flux of a full module after repeated cleaning cycles. Studies report flux before and after a single cleaning, and many report flux on small coupons that were never cleaned. The cumulative effect of cleaning on module performance is not reported, although cleaning is a principal operating cost of a membrane plant and the deployment question turns on it. A membrane that recovers its flux fully after each of many cleanings supports one design; a membrane that loses performance at every cycle supports another, with more membrane area, more frequent replacement, or a different process. The literature does not allow the reader to distinguish between the two.

The surrounding gaps are of the same kind. Long-duration studies are few beside the many short screening studies, and reports on genuine process streams are few beside reports on synthetic mixtures. The condition of membranes after service, and the failure mechanism that ended their service, are seldom described. The evidence base for solvent recovery by membranes is consequently narrower than the volume of publication suggests: it is deep on screening and on short-term behaviour, and thin on exactly the long-term, module-scale, cleaned-and-reused performance on which an industrial decision would rest.

The scope has a consequence the reader should hold in mind. Because the set is limited to examined journal work, it describes what researchers have chosen to study and publish, not what plants have chosen to install. Solvent recovery duties that reached operation without generating a publication are absent, and duties that failed early are absent with them. The established results below are therefore established for the systems studied, under the conditions reported, and the extension of any of them to an unstudied solvent or an unreported membrane is an inference the literature itself does not make.

A further point of agreement concerns reporting practice rather than performance. Most studies condition a new membrane before measurement and report the conditioning, most report the feed composition and the temperature, and most state whether the feed was a synthetic mixture or a process stream. This consistency of reporting is what makes the disagreements in the next section informative: where reports conflict on an outcome while agreeing on the description of what was done, the cause is more likely to sit in a variable that none of them reports than in sloppy description by one side.

The disagreement also has a practical edge. A designer who believes the stable account sizes the plant with little spare membrane area and a modest cleaning provision; a designer who believes the declining account installs spare area, provides for frequent cleaning, or rejects the membrane option at the outset. The two accounts therefore lead to different plants and different costs from the same evidence, and the conflict is not an academic one. It sits inside every estimate prepared from this literature, usually invisibly, because the estimator adopts one account by adopting one subset of the papers as representative.

The gaps share a common cause. Screening studies are quick and publishable; long studies tie up equipment and produce their result slowly; module studies require hardware that many laboratories do not own; cleaning studies produce wear that a laboratory may prefer not to inflict on a scarce membrane sample. The literature is shaped by these incentives, and the thin places in the record are thin for reasons that have nothing to do with their importance to a decision. Naming the cause matters because it indicates the remedy: the missing measurements will not appear as a by-product of more screening work, and a reader who needs them must either commission them or proceed without them, knowing which choice was made.
